title: Irrigation water demand: A meta-analysis of price elasticities
authors: Susanne M. Scheierling, John B. Loomis, Robert A. Young
finding: "The mean price elasticity is 0.48." (abstract; elasticity reported in absolute value, from 24 U.S. studies since 1963)
unit: coefficient (absolute price elasticity of irrigation water demand)
conversion: Absolute value of the meta-sample mean price elasticity used directly as the model's response coefficient; the model's (0.4 x charge / net value) form is a first-order linear-demand equivalent of an elasticity
strengthWhy: Direct meta-analysis of the exact quantity (price elasticity of irrigation water demand) across US studies; mechanism match is exact, but it is a pooled mean rather than a Utah/GSL-basin estimate
differencesFromUtah: Pooled across US regions, crops and decades (1963 onward); mostly short-run; authors note long-run elasticities are likely larger and high-value crops less elastic. Utah's low-value alfalfa/hay-dominated mix sits at the more elastic end, but Utah water law (prior appropriation, shares via irrigation companies, use-it-or-lose-it) means growers often face near-zero marginal water price, so response to a new charge is untested.
verification: WebFetch of the EarthRef reference record returned the abstract with the quoted mean; citation (authors/year/journal/DOI) confirmed on the same page

title: Price and Income Elasticities of Residential Water Demand: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Jasper M. Dalhuisen, Raymond J. G. M. Florax, Henri L. F. de Groot, Peter Nijkamp
finding: "The distribution of price elasticities has a sample mean of -.41, a median of -.35, and a standard deviation of .86." and "providing substantial evidence for water demand being price inelastic."
conversion: Absolute value of the reported mean (-0.41); minus signs are mangled to '2' in the PDF text layer, read in context against the accompanying median and standard deviation
strengthWhy: Exact quantity (price elasticity of residential water demand) measured directly, but residential only - not industrial or commercial - and the pooled mean is 0.41 versus the model's 0.3
differencesFromUtah: Meta-sample spans many countries and decades; Utah has among the highest per-capita municipal use and lowest water rates in the US, and a large outdoor-irrigation share, which typically makes demand MORE price-responsive than this pooled mean.
verification: Downloaded the publisher PDF via WebFetch, ran pdftotext and grepped page 295; quoted sentence read directly from the extracted text

title: Economic Determinants of Industrial Water Demand: A Review of the Applied Research Literature
place: International review of industrial water demand studies
finding: "One of the conclusions drawn from the results is that the water demand for industrial uses is inelastic (direct price elasticity usually less than the unit), although this elasticity is greater than in the domestic case."
location: page 16 of 23, Section 5 discussion (Table 4 holds the individual estimates)
conversion: Qualitative bound only: the review states industrial elasticities are below 1 in absolute value but above residential ones. Combined with the Dalhuisen residential mean of 0.41, this brackets a blended M&I elasticity near the assumed 0.3-0.5; no single pooled number is reported.
strengthWhy: Covers the industrial/commercial half of the M&I assumption, which the residential meta-analyses miss, but it is a narrative review with no pooled mean, and the studies are mostly European
differencesFromUtah: Mostly Spanish, French and Canadian firm-level studies; no Utah or Great Basin case. The review notes water is a tiny share of firm costs, which is even more true in Utah where water is cheap, so a charge big enough to bite would have to be large.
verification: Downloaded the MDPI article PDF with curl, pdftotext, grepped 'price elasticity'; quoted sentence read from extracted page 16

title: 2026/2027 ADOPTED Water Rates Summary - Wholesale Water Rates (Non-Pumped), rate per acre foot
place: Salt Lake County, Utah (Great Salt Lake basin)
finding: "WHOLESALE WATER RATES (NON-PUMPED) ... (Rate per Acre Foot)": 2026/2027 member-agency rates run from Magna Water District $476.29 and Taylorsville-Bennion $474.11 up to Draper Irrigation (Water Pro) $811.41; BCWTP rate $557.19.
location: page 1, Wholesale Water Rates (Non-Pumped) table, 2026/2027 RATES column
conversion: Read directly in $/acre-foot, no conversion. Simple midpoint of the 14 member-agency rates listed is roughly $600/AF. Cross-check: the retail Tier 1 non-pumped rate of $1.53 per 1,000 gallons equals about $499/AF (x 325.851 thousand gallons per AF).
strengthWhy: The exact quantity, for the largest municipal wholesaler in the Great Salt Lake basin, in the model's own unit and for the current year

Caveat: these are wholesale rates to member cities (cost of treated, delivered water including capital), not the shadow value of a raw water right; smaller rural Utah systems and self-supplied industry pay less. The figure is about 1.6x the model's assumed $380/AF.

title: How Agricultural Water Conservation Can Save the Great Salt Lake
authors: Man Li and Asif Ahmed Khan
place: Bear, Weber and Jordan watersheds, Utah (Great Salt Lake tributaries)
publisher: Choices Magazine, Agricultural & Applied Economics Association, Vol. 39 Quarter 4
verification: curl of the AgEcon Search PDF, pdftotext -layout, quotes read from pages 4-5
finding: "Additionally, all farmers in Jordan and Bear watersheds would fallow their irrigated alfalfa fields-45,600 acres and 13,200 acres, respectively-regardless of the payment level. In contrast, only half of irrigated alfalfa acres in Weber, approximately 95,200 acres, would be fallowed."
location: page 5, 'Where Is It Worth Conserving?' section
conversion: Indirect. The authors' willingness-to-accept supply curve shows that fallowing ALL irrigated alfalfa in the three GSL tributary watersheds yields 512.5 KAF of reduced withdrawals, and that at feasible payment levels only about half of Weber's alfalfa acres (the highest-cost watershed) respond. Against agriculture's roughly 0.9 MAF of basin consumptive use (63% of 1.46 MAF in 2016, same paper), a full-alfalfa-fallow price response is on the order of half to two-thirds of agricultural use, bracketing the assumed 0.60 cap.
strengthWhy: Same place, same crop, same mechanism (a money signal applied to GSL-basin irrigators) and it does show a saturating response curve - but it prices VOLUNTARY fallowing payments, not a charge on water use, and the cap has to be inferred from the supply curve rather than read off a table
differencesFromUtah: None geographically - this is the GSL basin. The difference is instrument (payment to fallow vs charge on use) and crop scope (irrigated alfalfa only, so other crops' potential is excluded, which biases the implied cap DOWN).

conversion: None needed - the authors already converted to $/AF. $456/AF is the LOWEST lowest-tier municipal rate in the GSL study area; the assumed $380/AF sits below the bottom of the observed range.
